A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniTraj research despite the changed title and organization. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Basketball-U, Football-U and Soccer-U, including baseline comparisons, component ablations and architecture studies in the main text and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds pedestrian-prediction and traffic-imputation results in Appendix E, together with qualitative trajectory comparisons.

M1.justification: Equation (4) revises the stated GSM computation: v1 directly max-pools the repeated binary mask, whereas v2 applies an MLP/linear projection before pooling. The CVAE framework, bidirectional Mamba/BTS, decoder and losses otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix E adds ETH-UCY and SDD pedestrian trajectory prediction and Traffic-Guangzhou time-series imputation. These substantially extend evaluation beyond the three retained sports datasets into different populations and data domains.

E2.justification: New reported comparisons include MemoNet, FlowChain and EqMotion on ETH-UCY; MemoNet and FlowChain on SDD; and CSBI and BayOTIDE on Traffic-Guangzhou. These add substantial specialist comparator coverage. The existing sports comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce minFDE20 for pedestrian prediction and RMSE/MAE for traffic imputation. The retained sports splits, masking strategies, K=20 sampling and training settings are unchanged. Splits, prediction horizons and traffic masking settings for the new evaluations are not specified.

E4.justification: v2 adds two Basketball-U qualitative case studies in Figures 4 and 5, comparing missing-location reconstruction, trajectory smoothness and court-boundary behavior. Existing component, pooling, depth and temporal-architecture ablations are retained unchanged. The additional benchmark scores do not establish a separate controlled robustness study.

E5.justification: Both versions specify training seed 2024 and report point estimates without confidence intervals, repeated-run variability or significance tests. The new result tables retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: The sports benchmark and ablation values are retained. New Tables 10–12 report UniTraj minADE20/minFDE20 of 0.23/0.36 averaged over ETH-UCY and 8.68/12.78 on SDD, plus Traffic-Guangzhou RMSE/MAE of 3.942/2.784. Qualitative findings are also added. These are additional results under new settings, not improvements over v1's matched sports results.

T1.justification: Equation (4) changes the mathematical definition of the ghost embedding by inserting a learned projection inside max-pooling. The likelihood, ELBO, temporal recurrence and loss formulations remain unchanged; Equation (7)'s combined bidirectional notation is equivalent to its earlier form. No new proofs or theoretical guarantees appear.

C1.justification: The title, abstract and conclusion explicitly narrow the emphasis to sports, and the abstract removes v1's claim to be the first work addressing the unified problem. The central contributions—unified trajectory generation, GSM/BTS and three sports benchmarks—remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 suggests that player counts and court sizes explain differing component contributions across sports. Appendix E acknowledges weaker results than some specialists and proposes differences in interaction structure as an explanation for traffic results. The existing limitations concerning the simple decoder and fixed agent counts are retained.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the GSM projection in Equation (4) as a linear layer. Otherwise, implementation configurations, hardware, optimizer, training budget and code/data/checkpoint link targets remain unchanged. The added benchmarks receive little corresponding implementation or adaptation documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new benchmarks and comparisons, develops the sports-versus-pedestrian distinction, and adds a substantive comparison with the already-cited Traj-MAE. It removes discussions of Motion Mamba, Traj-LLM and Simple-Mamba. The three principal related-work themes remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled Sports-Traj, the abstract and introduction are reworked around sports interactions, and Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 4 after experiments. Expanded encoder explanations and new qualitative/generalizability subsections substantially reorganize the narrative, alongside citation-style and conference-header changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds two eight-panel qualitative figures and three benchmark tables, substantially expanding the visual evidence. It also corrects the architecture diagram's classification from Table 1 to Figure 2 and the ablation displays from Figures 3–4 to Tables 3–4. Existing displays are resized or relocated within the conference layout.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's sports-only evidence, v2 provides useful outside-sports comparisons and qualitative examples that make applicability and trajectory behavior easier to assess. Sports-specific framing and corrected display references also improve clarity. The gain is limited because Appendix E omits key protocols and adaptations for the added benchmarks, so the new results only partly resolve the earlier gap in evidence for broader applicability.
